english: I don't think I can make it today
usage: I don't think I can make it today
Polite; the soft, standard way to back out of plans
I don't think I can come today
I'm afraid I won't be able to attend today
Formal 합쇼체, to a boss or in a work message
오늘 참석 못 할 것 같아요
I don't think I can attend today
참석하다 ('attend') for a meeting/event rather than a casual hangout
examples: 미안한데 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요.
Sorry, but I don't think I can make it today.
Open with 미안한데 ('sorry, but') to cushion the bad news
저 오늘 좀 아파서 못 갈 것 같아요.
I'm a bit sick today, so I don't think I can come.
좀 아파서 ('a bit sick, so') gives a brief reason before the -아서
죄송한데 오늘 회식에 못 갈 것 같습니다. 갑자기 일이 생겨서요.
I'm sorry, but I don't think I can come to the team dinner today — something came up.
회식 (work dinner) + formal 같습니다, with 갑자기 일이 생겨서요 as the reason
nuance: 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요 is 못 ('cannot') + 가다 ('to go') + -ㄹ 것 같다 ('it seems / I think'), so literally 'it seems I can't go today.' The whole trick is the -ㄹ 것 같다 hedge: Korean almost never says a flat 못 가요 ('I can't go') to cancel, because that sounds blunt and final, almost rude. Wrapping it in 같아요 ('I think / it seems') softens it into a gentle, apologetic 'I don't think I can make it' — even when you are 100% sure you can't go, you still say 같아요. This is the single most useful cancel-line a newcomer needs. The near alternative 안 갈 것 같아요 uses 안 ('won't, by choice') instead of 못 ('can't, prevented'), and that difference matters: 못 가요 means something is stopping you (work, illness), which sounds like a valid excuse, while 안 가요 means you simply choose not to go, which can sound like you just don't want to — so for canceling, default to 못. The classic English-speaker pitfall is translating 'I can't make it' word-for-word and dropping the hedge, producing a cold 오늘 못 가요; add 것 같아요 and a 미안한데/죄송한데 opener. Register: 같아요 (polite) for most people, 같습니다 for work/superiors, 같아 only with close friends.

Mistranslating 'make it' literally with 만들다.
'Make it' here is idiomatic English for 'attend'. 만들다 means 'to build/create' — never 오늘 못 만들어요. Use 못 가요/못 갈 것 같아요.

usage: Polite; the all-purpose vague reason for canceling
반말 / trailing reason, to a friend
An urgent matter suddenly came up
Add 급한 ('urgent') to stress it's serious and unavoidable
집에 ('at home') hints at a family matter without details
examples: 갑자기 일이 생겨서요. 다음에 봬요.
Something came up, so… Let's meet next time.
Trailing -서요 lets the excuse stand alone, softly
미안, 갑자기 일이 생겨서 오늘 못 갈 것 같아.
Sorry, something came up so I don't think I can come today.
반말 to a friend, chaining the reason into the cancel
죄송합니다, 갑자기 급한 일이 생겨서 오늘 미팅 참석이 어려울 것 같습니다.
I'm sorry — an urgent matter suddenly came up, so I don't think I can attend today's meeting.
Formal work register with 급한 일 and 참석이 어렵다
nuance: 갑자기 일이 생겨서요 is 갑자기 ('suddenly') + 일 ('a matter/thing/work') + 생기다 ('to arise/come up') + -어서 ('because') + 요 (polite ender), i.e. 'because something suddenly came up.' This is the socially perfect vague excuse: 일 is deliberately broad — it can mean work, an errand, a family thing, anything — so you can bow out without disclosing private details, and Koreans accept it without prying. The trailing -서요 (reason + 요, with the main clause left unsaid) is extremely natural and polite; it implies '…so I can't make it' without you having to spell out the blunt part. Watch the verb: it must be 생기다 ('to arise', intransitive), so 일이 생겼어요 ('a matter arose'); learners wrongly use 만들다 ('make') and say 일을 만들었어요, which means 'I created trouble/work' — wrong nuance entirely. Particle trap: it's 일이 (subject) with 생기다, not 일을. Compare 바빠서요 ('because I'm busy'), which is fine but can sound like a weaker brush-off; 일이 생겨서요 implies a concrete unforeseen event and lands as a stronger, more legitimate reason. The 갑자기 ('suddenly') is what signals this wasn't your fault — keep it.

english: Would it be okay to cancel our plans?
usage: Would it be okay to cancel our plans?
Is it okay if I cancel?
Would it be alright to cancel?
괜찮을까요 ('would it be alright') is a touch gentler
Would it be a problem if I canceled today?
examples: 미안한데 오늘 약속 취소해도 될까요?
Sorry, but would it be okay to cancel today's plans?
미안한데 softens the request before asking permission
나 컨디션이 너무 안 좋은데 약속 취소해도 돼?
I'm really not feeling well — is it okay if I cancel?
반말 with 컨디션이 안 좋다 ('feeling off') as the reason
정말 죄송한데 갑자기 일이 생겨서 오늘 약속 취소하면 안 될까요?
I'm really sorry, but something came up — would it be a problem if I canceled today?
The 안 될까요 negative form sounds the most apologetic
nuance: 약속 취소해도 될까요? is 약속 ('plans/an appointment/a promise') + 취소하다 ('to cancel', Sino-Korean 取消) + -아도 되다 ('is it okay to…') + -ㄹ까요 ('I wonder, may I?'). Framing the cancellation as a permission question — 'would it be okay if…' — is the polite, face-saving move: instead of announcing you ARE canceling, you ask whether you may, handing the other person dignity. Note 약속 is a big, important word: it covers plans to meet, an appointment, AND a promise, so canceling 약속 carries a slight weight of breaking your word — which is exactly why you ask so gently. The near alternative 약속 취소할게요 ('I'll cancel our plans', with -ㄹ게요) just DECLARES the cancellation and can feel one-sided/abrupt for plans with another person; reserve 취소할게요 for impersonal bookings (a reservation, a delivery). The negative-question variant 취소하면 안 될까요? ('would it be a problem if I canceled?') sounds even more pleading and apologetic — handy when you feel bad. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) saying 약속을 깨다 ('break the appointment') — 깨다 is harsh, literally 'shatter the promise', and sounds like a serious betrayal; use 취소하다 for a normal cancel. (2) Treating 약속 as only 'a promise' and avoiding it for plans — it's the right word for 'our plans to meet'.

약속 also means 'plans/an appointment to meet'. 'Cancel our plans' is 약속 취소하다 — it's the correct everyday word, not just for breaking a vow.

english: Could we change the time of our plans?
usage: Could we change our meeting time?
Polite; asking to move the time, not cancel
변경하다 (Sino-Korean) sounds more formal/official than 바꾸다
Could we push the time back just a little?
미루다 ('postpone') when you want it slightly later, not a different slot
examples: 혹시 약속 시간 좀 바꿔도 될까요?
Could we possibly change our meeting time?
혹시 ('by any chance') softens the request
나 길이 막혀서 그런데 약속 시간 30분만 늦춰도 돼?
I'm stuck in traffic — can we push it 30 minutes later?
30분만 늦추다 ('push back just 30 min') for a small delay
죄송한데 회의 시간 좀 변경해도 될까요? 오전은 일정이 꽉 차서요.
Sorry, could we change the meeting time? My morning is fully booked.
변경하다 + reason 일정이 꽉 차다 ('schedule is packed')
nuance: 약속 시간 좀 바꿔도 될까요? is 약속 시간 ('meeting time') + 좀 (softener) + 바꾸다 ('to change/swap') + -아도 될까요 ('may I…?'). Crucial distinction from the previous card: this CHANGES the time but KEEPS the plan, whereas 취소 cancels it — and Koreans much prefer rescheduling to canceling, so this is the friendlier ask. 바꾸다 is the everyday verb for 'change/swap'; the Sino-Korean 변경하다 means the same but is more formal and shows up in business/official contexts (변경하다 a flight, a meeting, a reservation). If you specifically want it LATER, the precise verb is 미루다 or 늦추다 ('postpone/push back'); if EARLIER, 당기다 ('move up'). The 좀 here is a politeness lubricant, not 'a little' — though you can add 조금만 ('just a little') for a small shift: 시간 조금만 바꿔도 될까요?. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) using 바꾸다 with the wrong particle pattern — say 시간을 바꾸다 ('change the time'), and to swap A for B it's A를 B로 바꾸다 (e.g. 3시를 5시로 바꾸다, 'change 3 to 5'); learners drop the -로 on the new time. (2) Saying 시간을 옮기다 — 옮기다 ('move/relocate') is more for physically moving things or moving a date/venue (날짜를 옮기다 works), but for the clock time, 바꾸다/미루다 is more natural.

To replace A with B you mark the new value with -로: 3시를 5시로 바꿔도 될까요? ('change 3 to 5'). Without -로 it's incomplete.
Using formal 변경하다 with a close friend.
변경하다 is Sino-Korean and sounds official/business-like. With friends use the everyday 바꾸다: 시간 좀 바꿔도 돼?
Saying 시간을 옮기다 for the clock time.
옮기다 ('move/relocate') fits dates or venues (날짜를 옮기다) better than the time of day. For the time, prefer 바꾸다 or, for 'later', 미루다/늦추다.

english: Could we push it to another day?
usage: Could we move it to another day?
Polite; asks to postpone to a different day
Can we do it another day?
Would it be possible to push it to another day?
-ㄹ 수 있을까요 ('would it be possible') is a touch softer/formal
Could we move it to next week?
Swap in a concrete time (다음 주 'next week') instead of vague 다른 날
examples: 오늘은 좀 힘들 것 같은데, 다른 날로 미뤄도 될까요?
Today's a bit hard — could we move it to another day?
오늘은 힘들 것 같다 sets up the postpone request
미안, 나 이번 주 너무 바빠서 다른 날로 미뤄도 돼?
Sorry, I'm so busy this week — can we do it another day?
반말 with a busy-week reason
죄송한데 다음 주로 미룰 수 있을까요? 그때는 꼭 시간 낼게요.
Sorry, could we push it to next week? I'll definitely make time then.
꼭 시간 낼게요 ('I'll be sure to make time') shows good faith
nuance: 다른 날로 미뤄도 될까요? is 다른 날 ('another day') + -로 (direction particle, 'to') + 미루다 ('to postpone/put off') + -아도 될까요 ('may I…?'). 미루다 is THE verb for postponing — pushing an event to a later point — and it's the heart of polite rescheduling. The particle -로 on 다른 날 ('to another day') is essential and exactly where learners slip: you move it TO a day, so 다른 날로, 다음 주로, 주말로; dropping the -로 (saying 다른 날 미뤄도 될까요) sounds off. Two contrasts to know: (1) 미루다 vs. 취소하다 — 미루다 keeps the plan alive for later (much preferred socially), 취소하다 kills it; reach for 미루다 whenever you can still meet, just not now. (2) 미루다 vs. 연기하다 — 연기하다 (Sino-Korean 延期) means the same 'postpone' but is formal/official (postponing an event, a wedding, a match: 경기가 연기됐다); for casual plans use 미루다, for official announcements use 연기하다/연기되다. English-speaker pitfall: 미루다 can also mean 'to procrastinate/keep putting off' (일을 자꾸 미루다 = 'keep putting work off'), so in the right frame it's neutral 'reschedule', but be aware tone — paired with a reason and 다른 날로 it clearly means 'postpone to another day', not 'I'm lazily delaying'. Don't confuse 미루다 with 밀다 ('to push physically').

usage: 뵙다 (humble 'see') to an elder/superior; very respectful
Let's see each other again sometime
또 ('again') warms it up, keeps the door open
examples: 오늘은 아쉽지만 다음에 봬요.
It's a shame about today, but let's meet another time.
아쉽지만 ('it's a pity, but') keeps the cancel warm
알겠어, 그럼 다음에 봐!
Got it, see you next time then!
반말 reply accepting a reschedule
오늘 정말 죄송했습니다. 다음에 꼭 뵐게요.
I'm really sorry about today. I'll be sure to see you next time.

nuance: 다음에 봬요 is 다음에 ('next time / another time') + 봬요 (the contracted polite form of 뵈어요, from 뵙다, the humble verb 'to see/meet someone respectfully'). This is the gentle sign-off that softens a cancellation — by promising a future meeting, it signals 'no hard feelings, we'll still get together.' The spelling/sound is a notorious trap: 봬요 (= 뵈어요) is correct, NOT 뵈요; in speech both sound like 'bwae-yo', but 뵈요 is a misspelling — many natives get this wrong too. Register nuance: 뵙다 is humble (you lower yourself before the person you're meeting), so 봬요/뵐게요 is warmer and more respectful than the plain 봐요/볼게요 (from 보다). To an elder, boss, or someone you respect, 다음에 뵐게요 is lovely; among peers 다음에 봬요 or casual 다음에 봐 is fine. The near alternative 다음에 만나요 (from 만나다 'to meet') is also correct and a bit more neutral/direct, but 봬요 carries that humble politeness. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) writing 뵈요 instead of 봬요. (2) Treating 'next time' literally and pinning a date — 다음에 is intentionally vague ('sometime'), a friendly soft promise, not a commitment to a specific next meeting; if you DO want a real plan, say 다음에 언제 볼까요? ('when shall we meet next?').
